card st-build-run  [decided]
The merge loop: queue one ticket, merge it, then run the held-out set
why: Each ticket is green alone. Only a check on the run's tree plus the ticket shows whether they are green together.
subtree: 15 cards, 1 open, 14 decided

The coordinator takes the finished tickets one at a time, through a merge queue. #st-build-run-mechanics gives how the merge loop does it.

1. Make a temporary tree: the run's tree plus the ticket.
2. Run every check on the temporary tree, once each. A red check does not stop the merge: the ticket merges, and a follow-up ticket is filed to fix the red check (#ms-merge-red-follow-up).
3. A merge conflict is the one failure that sends the ticket back to the builder loop, with the conflict (#st-build-conflict).
4. Run the held-out set on the run's tree. This step belongs to validate, not build (#st-validate-heldout). A red step files a follow-up ticket, and the merge stands.

Build ends when every ticket is merged and every held-out step passes (#st-g2-heldout).

  -> refines         st-build-steps  Build: a builder loop per ticket and a merge loop per run
  -> depends_on      st-build-ticket  The builder loop: one ticket, fresh passes until the checks, the grader, and the review pass
       why: The merge loop takes finished tickets from the builder loop of #st-build-ticket and sends a red merge back to it.
  -> depends_on      st-validate-heldout  The held-out set belongs to validate, and validate runs beside build
       why: The merge loop runs the held-out set as a validate step, as this card decides.
  -> depends_on      st-g2-heldout  G2 waits until every held-out step is green on the merged tree
       why: The merge loop ends build only when every held-out step passes, the G2 rule this card sets.

  <- depends_on      werk-loop  Inner build loop

  <- refines         st-build-run-cas  One werk instance runs in a repo, so a moved run branch needs no handling

There are 27 tickets in ready, and all of them are follow-ups or rework. Yes, some patterns are worth worrying about.

**What they are**
- **15 "Follow-up for werk/N: N.x"** come from the held-out set. A merged ticket's held-out step was red, so the merge loop filed a ticket (#st-build-run step 4).
- **10 "Rework werk/N: a decision it was built on changed"** (24 ×3, 27 ×4, 32 ×3, 21 ×1). A card that a builder proposed was later discarded or removed. Examples are `#werk-chat-cmdmenu-read` and `#st-spec-plan-folder`.
- **2 "Judge held-out steps of werk/17 against a card"** (17.4, 17.5). These are grader tickets for held-out steps.

**Patterns to worry about**
1. **Held-out red is the norm.** About 24 of 41 done tickets show it. A ticket passes its own checks and its own grader, and then the held-out set finds the gap. The builder loop checks less than it should.
2. **Duplicates.** Step 17.5 has tickets 54, 56 and 58, and 56 is building now. werk/23 has five follow-ups (55, 59, 66, 74, plus 23.1 and 23.2 together). Filing one ticket per step or per event repeats the same fix. Nothing dedupes them.
3. **Rework is one ticket per changed card.** werk/27 has four rework tickets. Each ticket cites 16 to 24 cards for a one-card change, so the scope is wide and the tickets overlap.
4. **The rework metric misses this.** `werk rework` reports 0 cited cards reopened. The real rework comes from discarded builder-proposed cards. That signal is invisible to the metric.
5. **A ticket body may be bound to the wrong ticket.** werk/68 is "Follow-up for werk/27", with cites about model selection. Its scenario is about `ticket archive` and `ticket restore`, which belongs to werk/29. I read only the first lines. Check this one by hand.
6. **No cap.** #st-build-run-cap sets no limit on follow-up tickets in v0. With the patterns above, the queue can grow faster than it drains.
7. **Blocked chain.** 13 tickets wait on werk/34 and werk/38. Both are still building.

**Cause of the rework:** builders propose cards for decisions nobody made. You then rule differently, and the code is already merged.

Next: tell me which to do first. I recommend a card for pattern 2 and 3, one follow-up per ticket and one rework per changed card. I can also check werk/68 first.
2 and 3 are good candidates. Please plan the fix, implement it and document decisions

--body "Problem. A merged ticket can need a fix more than once before the first fix is built. Its held-out steps can turn red one run after another, and the decisions it was built on can change one after another. Each event filed its own follow-up ticket, so one merged ticket got four or five open follow-ups. They cite the same cards, touch the same code, and conflict when they merge.

Answer. A merged ticket has at most one open follow-up of each kind. The kinds are the step follow-up, which makes red held-out steps green (#st-heldout-followup-per-ticket), and the rework, which brings the code in line with a decision that changed (#st-build-missing-decision). A follow-up is open until it is done or archived.

When a later problem of the same kind appears, one of three cases holds:
- There is no open follow-up of that kind. A new follow-up is filed, as before.
- The open follow-up is still in ready or blocked. It takes the new problem into itself: its text and its list of steps or changes are written again with the union, and no ticket is filed.
- The open follow-up has started to build. Its text is not changed under a running builder. A step follow-up files nothing, and the next held-out run after its merge sees the red steps again. A rework files a new ticket, because the change is not in the text the builder reads.

A follow-up that judges a held-out step against a decided card is a different kind and is not covered here.

Example:
- Ticket W is merged. It has held-out steps W.1, W.2 and W.3.
- F is the open step follow-up of W.

1. Held-out run 1: step W.1 is red. No follow-up of W is open, so F is filed with W.1.
2. Held-out run 2, F in ready: step W.2 is red. F takes it. F now carries W.1 and W.2.
3. F starts to build. Held-out run 3: step W.3 is red. F is building, so nothing is filed.
4. F merges. The next held-out run finds W.3 red and files a new follow-up G with W.3.

\`\`\`
run 1: W.1 red ----------> F (W.1)           file F
run 2: W.2 red ----------> F (W.1 W.2)       F in ready: join
run 3: W.3 red   F building: wait
F merges
run 4: W.3 red ----------> G (W.3)           no open follow-up: file G

F, G = follow-up tickets of W   W.n = held-out step n of W
\`\`\`" \

A merged ticket has at most one open follow-up of each kind, and a later problem joins it
why: A merged ticket can go wrong in the same code again and again: a second held-out step turns red, or a second decision it was built on changes. A new ticket for each event gives several tickets that change the same code at the same time. One open follow-up per ticket and kind takes each later problem into itself, so one builder fixes them together.

Problem. A merged ticket can need a fix more than once before the first fix is built. Its held-out steps can turn red one run after another, and the decisions it was built on can change one after another. Each event filed its own follow-up ticket, so one merged ticket got four or five open follow-ups. They cite the same cards, touch the same code, and conflict when they merge.

Answer. A merged ticket has at most one open follow-up of each kind. The kinds are the step follow-up, which makes red held-out steps green (#st-heldout-followup-per-ticket), and the rework, which brings the code in line with a decision that changed (#st-build-missing-decision). A follow-up is open until it is done or archived.

When a later problem of the same kind appears, one of three cases holds:
- There is no open follow-up of that kind. A new follow-up is filed.
- The open follow-up is still in ready or blocked. It takes the new problem into itself: its text and its list of steps or changes are written again with both, and no ticket is filed.
- The open follow-up has started to build. Its text does not change under a running builder. A step follow-up files nothing, and the next held-out run after its merge sees the red steps again. A rework files a new ticket, because the change is not in the text the builder reads.
